scope: MiniVectorDB (question 600081) development session. Contains the student's verbatim prompts and the real, unedited outputs of every verification run. Agent-authored analysis is labelled role=agent and must not be read as student evidence. Fields named student_analysis are null where the student has not yet supplied their own reasoning; those are marked pending, not claimed as verified understanding.
material_notes: Redaction: none needed; no credentials, tokens or personal data appear. All commands were executed in WSL Ubuntu-24.04 (Python 3.12.3, x86_64, g++ 13). Outputs are trimmed to the lines that carry the result; nothing is paraphrased.

user_prompts.content: https://open.oceanbase.com/train/detail/21?questionId=600081 发布了最新的加赛，请你继续尝试解决
我觉得这个判断对，你继续做吧
我觉得是A 距离计算：1.28M 次浮点减乘加。用 SSE2（4 float/指令）约 32 万条 SIMD 指令
我认为可以A和B同时推进A 继续抠查询那剩下的 0.2 ms（记录访问）——收益上限约 1.5×，但查询权重 2/3 B 把写入的 2 次 fsync 合成 1 次（把提交标记写进同一个记录文件）——写入可能快近 2×，但权重只有 1/3
省下的不是 commits.log 那点内容，是"第二个文件"这件事本身的块级代价：文件系统按块/页写，每个文件都要单独分配块、写元数据、走一遍落盘路径；两次 fsync 覆盖两个文件，就是两份块对齐放大和元数据写。合并成一个文件一次 fsync，提交标记搭记录文件的同一批块和同一次落盘走，第二份文件的块级写放大和元数据开销就没了，所以 I/O 降了 0.37 MiB。

我觉得最难的约束是"崩溃后不能部分生效"和"数据超内存还要精确 TopK"这两条的组合，但真正卡人的是前者。因为超内存 + 精确 TopK 是一个静态的算法/数据结构问题，可以离线想清楚；而"崩溃后不能部分生效"是对每一条写入路径的全局不变量——它不允许你把原子性当成一个局部优化，任何一次提速（比如 B 的合并 fsync、A 的索引替换）都必须重新证明这条不变量还成立。我的判断是：这道题的设计意图不是比谁单点快，而是比谁在"改性能"和"保住崩溃语义"之间做取舍时，证据链完整。所以我把"崩溃 6/6 仍全过"当成每次改动的准入条件，而不是最后补的回归项。

我猜写入那 0.653 s 里 fsync 本身占大头。下一步做：把单次 fsync 换成 fdatasync（提交标记和记录已在同一文件、同一批块，不需要 inode 元数据持久化），预测 write T 从 0.653 s 降到 0.50 s 左右（±0.05），I/O 不变或略降，崩溃 6/6 仍须全过。如果降不到，说明瓶颈不在 fsync 的元数据部分而在块落盘本身，那我就转去测批量提交合并。

同意，"批量合并"在官方口径下不可行——提交点由测试驱动，合并多个 COMMIT 就违反"响应发出前必须完成持久化"。我修正假设为：预分配文件 + fdatasync——文件大小不再增长，fdatasync 省掉每次提交的 size/inode 元数据刷写，只刷数据块。预测 write T 从 0.602 s 降到 0.56 ± 0.03 s，I/O 基本不变（5.6 MiB 量级），崩溃 6/6 仍须全过（并注明：这仍只证明恢复逻辑，不证明持久性，SIGKILL 测不出 fdatasync 与 fsync 的差异）。证伪分支：若落在 [0.53, 0.59] 噪声带内，说明主成本是每次提交的块分配/块数而非元数据，下一步转去测"减少每次提交的块数"——把提交标记和记录头对齐到同一块，预测再降 0.02–0.03 s。

conversations.content: Proposed two possible fixes for the post-crash transaction-id reuse defect: (a) never reuse a transaction id, (b) truncate uncommitted records during recovery. Stated a preference for (a) because an uncommitted transaction's records can be followed by a committed transaction's records (autocommit statements interleaved with an explicit transaction), so truncation would discard committed data. Asked the student whether this reasoning holds or whether a counter-example should be constructed.
我觉得这个判断对，你继续做吧

Recorded explicitly that agreement without an executed check only meets the 0.5 evidence tier, and that the 1.5-2 tiers require the student to explain a result, correct the approach and re-test. Continued with the memory-bound test instead of claiming a higher tier.

Background given before the student's prediction: the 0.597 ms/query hot path scans 10000 rows x 128 dims, and the four candidate cost sources are A distance arithmetic (1.28M float sub/mul/add, ~320k SSE2 instructions), B per-row schema offset walk to locate the vector, C per-row block-cache lookup (std::map plus a one-entry memo), D bounded top-K maintenance (only rows that enter the top 10 trigger a sort).
我觉得是A 距离计算：1.28M 次浮点减乘加。用 SSE2（4 float/指令）约 32 万条 SIMD 指令

Measured answers to the student's three questions: log2(10000)=13.29 so a red-black tree holds at most 26.6 levels and typically ~14; a lookup walks one pointer per level; but because keys were inserted ascending, libstdc++ placed nodes sequentially, so 0.0% of in-order neighbours are more than 64 bytes apart and sequential iteration costs only 3.4 ns/entry versus 90.9 ns for a random find. The prefetcher handles the streaming distance loop well.
我认为可以A和B同时推进

experiments.title: First engine run
experiments.hypothesis: A complete first implementation should pass most public cases.
experiments.output:
sql_crud: FAIL line 5: SELECT content FROM docs;: rows: [['']] != [['更新']]
transaction_commit: FAIL line 6: SELECT id, content FROM docs;: rows: [[0, '']] != [[1, '修改']]
vector_index_maintenance: FAIL line 7: rows: [[0, 0.0], [0, 0.0], [3, 2.0]] != [[4, 0.0], [3, 2.0], [1, 5.0]]
transaction_shutdown_rollback: FAIL line 6: rows: [] != [[1], [2], [3]]
experiments.result_summary: 14/20 pass. Every failure involved UPDATE or DELETE: primary keys read back as 0 and strings as empty.
experiments.agent_interpretation: Two independent defects: (1) the tail block of the record file was cached while still zero-filled, and an append then wrote into that same block without invalidating the cache, so reads returned zeros; (2) the autocommit wrapper computed autocommit before running the statement, so BEGIN itself was auto-committed, which turned the following in-transaction DELETE into an autocommitted statement.

experiments.title: After cache invalidation and autocommit scoping
experiments.output: transaction_failed_insert: FAIL line 9: SELECT id, content FROM docs ORDER BY id;: rows: [[1, '保留'], [2, '二'], [3, '三'], [4, '四']] != [[1, '保留'], [2, '二'], [3, '三']]
experiments.result_summary: 19/20 pass. The remaining failure appears only after --restart: row 4 was correctly absent before the restart but reappeared after it.
experiments.agent_interpretation: Statement-level rollback removed the row from the in-memory index but left its record in the file tagged with the still-open transaction id; when that transaction later committed, recovery made the aborted row visible. Fix: append a compensating record during statement rollback so replay ends in the correct state.

experiments.title: Data larger than the memory budget
experiments.hypothesis: A bounded block cache plus a primary-key-to-offset index should let the engine work with data far above the process memory cap. This was argued from the design but had not been measured.
experiments.output:
load: 2001 statements in 18.3s | on-disk 104.0 MiB | peak RSS 16.9 MiB | cap 64 MiB
query: 24 TopK in 45.99s (1916.4 ms/query) | peak RSS 24.3 MiB
PASS exact + filtered TopK match brute-force truth (24/24)
PASS recovery + TopK after restart (ready in 0.38s, peak RSS 23.8 MiB)
big-table suite: 0 failure(s)
experiments.result_summary: Correctness and the memory bound both hold: 104 MiB of data under a 64 MiB address-space cap, peak RSS 24.3 MiB, 24/24 TopK equal to brute-force truth. But the query cost is 1916.4 ms per query, i.e. the design was correct and the performance was unusable.

experiments.title: Isolating the query cost: query-vector parsing hoisted out of the row loop
experiments.hypothesis: L2_DISTANCE re-parsed the 128-component query literal for every row, which is O(dim) string parsing per row.
experiments.output:
query: 24 TopK in 3.74s (155.7 ms/query) | peak RSS 24.3 MiB
PASS exact + filtered TopK match brute-force truth (24/24)
big-table suite: 0 failure(s)
experiments.result_summary: 1916.4 -> 155.7 ms/query, a 12.3x improvement, with identical answers.

experiments.title: Remove one pread per row and the O(n) LRU scan
experiments.hypothesis: read_row issued a pread for the 13-byte record header even when the record was cached, i.e. 10000 syscalls per query; the block cache also searched a vector for LRU bookkeeping on every access.
experiments.output:
query : T=2.065s  B=0.00 MiB  M=10.0 MiB  (1000 queries, 2.065 ms/query)
recall@10 = 1.0000
experiments.result_summary: 5.375 -> 2.065 ms/query (2.6x). Header now read from the cache; LRU replaced by a one-entry memo plus clock eviction.

experiments.title: Attempt that did not help: skipping projection for non-qualifying rows
experiments.hypothesis: Two heap allocations per row (projection values and ordering keys) were assumed to dominate.
experiments.output:
query : T=2.139s  B=0.00 MiB  M=9.9 MiB  (1000 queries, 2.139 ms/query)
recall@10 = 1.0000
experiments.result_summary: 2.065 -> 2.139 ms/query: no improvement, within noise. The allocation hypothesis was wrong; the change was kept only because it is asymptotically better for large K, not because it measured faster.

experiments.title: float SIMD accumulation, then a zero-copy vector view
experiments.hypothesis: double accumulation halves SIMD width; and decode copied 512 bytes per row into a scratch vector even when the vector was not projected.
experiments.output:
after float 8-way partial sums: query : T=1.799s (1.799 ms/query) recall@10 = 1.0000
after zero-copy view:        query : T=1.267s (1.267 ms/query) recall@10 = 1.0000
experiments.result_summary: 5.375 -> 1.799 -> 1.267 ms/query. Accumulated float error over 128 terms stays far inside the 1e-5 comparison tolerance; all 1000 answers still equal the double-precision brute-force truth.

experiments.title: Full regression after the zero-copy change
experiments.hypothesis: A zero-copy view into a cached block can alias stale memory; every path where a value escapes the scan must own its bytes.

experiments.title: Specialised TopK hot path: first attempt returned the FARTHEST rows
experiments.hypothesis: The generic scan builds Values and dispatches expressions per row. For vector TopK with a scalar filter the distance can be computed straight from the cached record bytes, removing all allocation and dispatch from the hot loop.
experiments.output:
write : T=0.794s  B=6.04 MiB  M=5.2 MiB
query : T=0.599s  B=0.00 MiB  M=9.8 MiB  (1000 queries, 0.599 ms/query)
recall@10 = 0.0000
JSON {... "exact": 0, "nq": 1000}
experiments.result_summary: 2.1x faster but recall@10 collapsed to 0.0000: every answer was wrong. The sort comparator was inverted, so the bounded top-K kept the K FARTHEST rows instead of the nearest.
experiments.agent_interpretation: std::sort with comp(a,b)=a.d>b.d orders descending, so top[0] was the worst row and the eviction test compared against the best. The comparator must order best-first so that top.back() is the evictable worst.

experiments.title: Ablation to test the student's prediction that distance arithmetic dominates
experiments.student_hypothesis: 我觉得是A 距离计算：1.28M 次浮点减乘加。用 SSE2（4 float/指令）约 32 万条 SIMD 指令
experiments.hypothesis: Student predicts A (distance arithmetic) is the dominant cost. Design: a standalone microbenchmark replicates the hot loop with components switched on cumulatively - mode0 pure distance over a contiguous array, mode1 adds the per-row schema offset walk, mode2 adds a per-row std::map lookup, mode3 adds bounded top-K maintenance. Same 10000x128 data, same 1000 queries, same 8-way float accumulation.
experiments.output:
mode0 distance only (contiguous)          0.121 ms/query   (total 0.121 s)
mode1 + per-row offset walk               0.129 ms/query   (total 0.129 s)
mode2 + per-row std::map lookup           0.500 ms/query   (total 0.500 s)
mode3 + bounded top-K (full shape)        0.514 ms/query   (total 0.514 s)
experiments.result_summary: Distance arithmetic alone is 0.121 ms/query, i.e. 24% of the 0.514 ms full shape. Adding the per-row schema offset walk costs only +0.008 ms. Adding a per-row std::map lookup costs +0.371 ms (72% of the total). Bounded top-K maintenance costs +0.014 ms. The student's prediction that A dominates is therefore refuted: C (map traversal) dominates. The engine's measured 0.597 ms/query is consistent with mode3 plus JSON/protocol overhead.
experiments.agent_interpretation: Initial reading was that C (map traversal) dominates. That reading was later weakened by E20: the ablation used random map::find, while the engine iterates the map in order, and E20 measured sequential iteration at only 3.4 ns/entry. See E20/E21 for the corrected picture.

experiments.title: What a std::map lookup actually costs (measured, not textbook)
experiments.hypothesis: The agent claimed map pointer-chasing explains the gap. Test it by measuring tree size, node locality, sequential iteration cost, random find cost, and a contiguous array scan.
experiments.output:
N                      = 10000
log2(N)                = 13.29   (RB-tree height bound 2*log2(N+1) = 26.6)
node address span      = 624.9 KiB across 10000 nodes
adjacent-in-order nodes farther than 64B apart = 0 / 9999 (0.0%)
sequential map iterate = 3.4 ns/entry
random map::find       = 90.9 ns/lookup
contiguous array scan  = 0.23 ns/entry
iterate / array        = 14.9x
experiments.result_summary: Because keys were inserted in ascending order, libstdc++ allocated nodes sequentially, so in-order neighbours are 0.0% farther than a cache line apart. Sequential iteration is 3.4 ns/entry (0.034 ms per 10000-row scan), while random find is 90.9 ns (27x). The ablation's mode2 used random find and therefore overstated the engine's cost. The agent's own 'map dominates' explanation is refuted by this measurement.

experiments.title: Split parse/protocol from scan using LIMIT 0
experiments.hypothesis: LIMIT 0 runs the same JSON parse, SQL lexer/parser and query-vector literal parse but skips the scan loop, so it measures the per-query floor.
experiments.output:

LIMIT 10 (parse+protocol+scan)       0.596 ms/query   (1000 queries, 0.596 s)
short SQL, no vector literal         0.055 ms/query

Pure distance arithmetic over a contiguous array is 0.121 ms (E19 mode0) and over the real 528-byte record layout with the offset walk is 0.129 ms (mode1). So about 0.39 ms of the scan is record-access bookkeeping that is NOT yet isolated. Both the student's hypothesis (A dominates) and the agent's first explanation (map traversal dominates) are only partly supported.

experiments.title: Both remaining candidates refuted: single block lookup + hoisted column offsets
experiments.hypothesis: The unexplained ~0.39 ms is either the two cache_.get calls per row or the second per-row schema walk for the filter column.

recall@10 = 1.0000

experiments.title: Compile-time dimension specialisation, and the out-of-bounds bug it introduced
experiments.hypothesis: The ablation used DIM=128 as a compile-time constant so GCC fully unrolled and vectorised; the engine used a runtime dim, leaving a remainder loop and narrower vectorisation.
experiments.output:
after l2_fixed<D> dispatch: query T=0.427s (0.427 ms/query) recall@10 = 1.0000
public suite: 19   <-- REGRESSION
after removing D=2 and D=4 cases: public suite 20, query T=0.401s (0.401 ms/query), recall@10 = 1.0000, crash suite 0 failure(s)
experiments.result_summary: 0.597 -> 0.427 ms confirmed the hypothesis. But the first version dropped the public suite to 19/20: l2_fixed<D> steps 8 floats per iteration, so D=2 and D=4 read past the end of the vector. Removing those cases (small dims fall back to the scalar path) restored 20/20 and gave 0.401 ms/query. Cumulative query improvement 5.375 -> 0.401 ms = 13.4x.
experiments.agent_interpretation: A performance specialisation silently broke correctness for small dimensions, and only the full public suite caught it - the 10000x128 benchmark alone would have looked like a pure win.

The 12-byte commit marker was forcing a full 4 KiB block write plus its own metadata path on every commit; folding it into the record file removes that block.

experiments.title: Transfer test: does the block-cost mechanism generalise to multi-table transactions?
experiments.hypothesis: If the student's block-amplification explanation is right, a transaction touching two tables must pay the second file's block cost again, because the single-fsync fold only applies when exactly one record file is dirty.

two-table      1335296 bytes / 100 commits =  13353 bytes per commit
experiments.result_summary: Two-table commits cost 13353 bytes versus 4628 for single-table, i.e. +8725 bytes per commit (about two extra 4 KiB blocks: the second record file plus commits.log and its metadata). The mechanism generalises, and it also shows the optimisation is correctly targeted: the official benchmark writes one table, which is exactly the case the fold covers.

experiments.title: Student-designed experiment: fsync -> fdatasync in the single-table commit

Falsification branch: if it does not drop, the cost is block flush rather than metadata, and the next step is batched commit merging.

experiments.verification_limitation: The crash suite uses SIGKILL, which does not discard the OS page cache, so it cannot distinguish fsync from fdatasync from no sync at all. The official crash model is also process-kill only (no power loss), so this suite validates the recovery logic, not durability itself. fdatasync is still safe here because Linux flushes a size increase, which is required for the appended bytes to be retrievable.

experiments.result_summary: Median write T = 0.630 s versus 0.602 s without preallocation. The student predicted 0.56 +/- 0.03 s, i.e. [0.53, 0.59]; the median falls above that band, and one run (0.592) lands inside it, so the 9% spread swamps the effect. Conclusion: preallocation gives no measurable benefit, so the size/inode metadata flush was not the cost either. The implementation was correct (crash 6/6, public 20/20, big-table 0 failures) but was REVERTED because it adds a preallocated-tail failure surface for zero gain. Both the student's prediction and the falsification band were missed, which points at per-commit block allocation/flush itself rather than metadata.

retrospective.what_was_hard: The public suite only exercises normal shutdown, so it cannot see crash-path defects. Two serious defects (stale tail-block cache, transaction-id reuse after a crash) were invisible to it and were only found by a self-written SIGKILL suite.
retrospective.what_did_not_work: Assuming per-row heap allocations dominated the query cost: measuring it showed no change (E12). Assuming the memory-bounded design implied acceptable performance: it was correct but 1916 ms/query (E8).
retrospective.measurement_discipline: Every performance claim is a wall-clock number from tests/bench.py or tests/big_table_test.py on the same generated data, with answers checked against double-precision brute-force truth. After E28 showed a 6% run-to-run spread and an optimistic 0.367 ms outlier, claims use the median of three runs, matching the official three-round rule.
student_contributions: Predicted that distance arithmetic dominated the query cost, with a quantitative SIMD instruction estimate; the ablation refuted it (E19).
Chose to pursue both the record-access and fsync optimisations against the agent's recommendation to stop optimising (E24).
Explained the I/O saving as second-file block amplification and metadata rather than payload bytes; confirmed quantitatively at 3973 bytes per commit versus a 4096-byte block (E24).

limitations: ann search mode currently executes the exact path, so Recall@10 is 1.0 but no approximate index is exercised.
The record file has no compaction, so it grows with updates.
The official baseline values, resource limits and hidden cases are not published, so the local benchmark optimises absolute T/B/M rather than the published efficiency ratio.
Local M is process peak RSS; the official metric also counts page cache, so local M is a lower bound.
The platform did not expose per-item T/B/M, a failure category, or Recall for the performance run, so the reason the performance entry did not reach the board is not yet determined.
pending_student_input: Every experiment above has student_analysis: null. The student has not yet supplied their own explanation of any result, so no instance above the 0.5 tier can be claimed from this material yet.
The only student judgement recorded so far is C2 (agreement with the transaction-id reasoning), which has no executed check attached and therefore belongs to the 0.5 tier at most.

To reach the higher tiers the student needs to state a hypothesis or objection in their own words, have it tested, then explain the result and any correction. Candidate open questions: why the query phase shows B=0 yet still costs 1.267 ms/query; whether float accumulation can reorder near-tied distances; whether the truncation alternative for transaction-id reuse really loses committed data.
